population.note: FICTIONAL. Of ~274M adults, 34.0% are current users (≈93.2M) and 46.0% have ever used (≈126M). Used-and-off-now is 12.0 pts (≈32.9M) and never-used is ≈148M. Ever-use rose 10.5 pts, inside the 12-pt limit. Cycling: ≈15.0 pts of current users are on a second or later course, mostly lapsed users re-enrolled by new Medicaid states and by switches to monthly MariTide. ≈4.5 pts of the off-now group restarted at least once and stopped again. So (15.0+4.5)/46.0 ≈ 42% have cycled. That is down from 45% because the denominator gained first-course users and monthly administered dosing improves persistence (MariTide one-year persistence ≈60% against ≈35–45% for weekly products). Age check: 18–29 16.5% × 52M = 8.6M; 30–49 41.1% × 91M = 37.4M; 50–64 51% × 61M = 31.1M; 65+ 23% × 70M = 16.1M; total ≈ 93.2M. The 18–29 band grew only 3 pts because the aesthetic inversion hit hardest there: 'fed' and 'built' bodies carry status, and in Austin, Brooklyn and Atlanta under-30 refusal is an identity, not a gap in access. Bottom third rose 21→31%, almost all through 9 more Medicaid states (40 + DC now on the continuation standard) and secondarily through ≈4.7M imported or counterfeit users, who are under-measured. Off-now (≈32.9M) breaks down roughly as follows: ≈9M stopped for GI or reward blunting ('the grey'), ≈8M lost coverage through private gating or missed verifications, ≈5M are on medically advised bone pauses or permanent stops (mostly 60+ women), ≈4M stopped because of cost or after generic entry failed to arrive, and ≈7M stopped by choice after reaching goal or by conviction. Never-users are increasingly young, rural residents of the 10 non-adopting states, people with contraindications, and the 'unmedicated' by identity. Pediatric: 1.0% of ~73M under-18s ≈ 730k, mostly adolescents 12+ on Medicaid EPSDT. Sponsors submitted the adolescent bone data FDA asked for in 2034, and it is under review. About two children in five now live with at least one parent who is on the drug or cycling.

access.public_coverage: FICTIONAL. The Part D obesity benefit is unchanged at the $199/month negotiated rate with a $50 beneficiary copay and the counselling visit. MariTide joined the Part D and Medicaid preferred tier at the same $199 rate (Amgen traded price for preferred placement, because administered monthly doses meet the continuation standard automatically). Medicare pays 18.8% of fills ≈ 17.5M users (16.1M aged 65+ plus ≈1.4M disabled under-65): ≈6.5M diabetes and ≈11.0M obesity. Obesity gross: 11.0M × $199 × 12 ≈ $26.3B. Beneficiaries pay 11.0M × $50 × 12 ≈ $6.6B, leaving ≈$19.7B/yr to the program. All Medicare incretin fills: 17.5M × $199 × 12 ≈ $41.8B gross. Medicaid: 40 states plus DC have adopted the continuation standard for the 90% match. The 9 new states (2033–34) include Pennsylvania, Michigan, Virginia, North Carolina and Arizona. Medicaid pays 18.8% of fills ≈ 17.5M × $199 × 12 ≈ $41.8B gross before supplemental rebates. Other public coverage (VA, TRICARE, and ACA marketplace plans in 12 states whose 2034 EHB benchmarks added anti-obesity medication) pays 4.3% ≈ 4.0M users. Public programmes together pay 41.9% of fills against 34.3% commercial and are the default payer for anyone over 65 or on low income.
access.generic_rest_of_world: India: 100+ semaglutide brands at $5–30/month, plus generic oral semaglutide and the first tirzepatide generics for domestic sale. China: domestic generic semaglutide and tirzepatide, and Chinese API still underlies most of the global gray trade. Canada: generic semaglutide at CAD 45–75/month. Brazil, Mexico, Turkey and Egypt have generics. US: the settlement entry date (2033) passed without an approved ANDA after FDA complete-response letters over peptide-impurity immunogenicity. Resubmissions are pending and no action is expected before 2035.
access.note: FICTIONAL. Stalled for a second step. The expected 2033 generic cliff did not arrive: FDA issued CRLs to the lead synthetic-semaglutide ANDAs (Apr 2033), so branded prices stayed where they were. Portal prices: injectable semaglutide and tirzepatide $199–279; orals $149–199; retatrutide $399 direct and $1,499 list; amycretin $449 direct; survodutide $379 direct; MariTide $349/month direct for an administered dose and $1,399 list. PBM net ≈ $170–190 under outcomes contracts. Payer mix of ≈93.2M users: commercial 34.3% (32.0M), Medicare 18.8% (17.5M), Medicaid 18.8% (17.5M), other public 4.3% (4.0M), cash/direct 18.8% (17.5M, including ≈4.0M 'calm'/'focus' subscribers and ≈0.6M off-label compulsion users), imported/counterfeit 5.0% (4.7M); sum 93.2M = 100%. Imports grew in absolute terms because the generic disappointment hit cash-paying uninsured users and those in the 10 non-adopting states. ≈78% of covering employers now gate, and ≈40% of those require ≥90% PDC, stricter than CMS's 80%. US market ≈ 88.5M paying users × ≈$185 average net × 12 ≈ $196B. Monthly products are ≈14% of US users (≈13M), mostly MariTide. The 503B exclusion and 503A injunction stand.

on_market_classes: GLP-1 agonist, weekly injectable (semaglutide: Wegovy/Ozempic, incl. 7.2 mg)
GIP/GLP-1 dual agonist, weekly injectable (tirzepatide: Zepbound/Mounjaro)
GIP/GLP-1/glucagon triple agonist, weekly injectable (retatrutide, incl. 12 mg maintenance)
GLP-1/glucagon dual agonist, weekly injectable (survodutide, approved Mar 2033)
GLP-1 + amylin analogue combination, weekly injectable (CagriSema)
GLP-1 agonist / GIPR antagonist antibody conjugate, monthly injectable (maridebart cafraglutide: MariTide, approved Feb 2033)
GLP-1 agonist, daily oral peptide (Wegovy pill, Rybelsus)
GLP-1 agonist, daily injectable (liraglutide: Saxenda, incl. generics)
mainstream_offlabel_uses: gambling-disorder and compulsive-betting treatment with low-dose oral semaglutide, reimbursed off-label by problem-gambling funds in Ohio, New Jersey, Massachusetts and Illinois (≈0.6M users); sNDA under priority review
compulsive shopping, pornography and 'doomscroll' craving reduction, prescribed by telehealth addiction services
smoking and vaping cessation (SHAPS-endpoint trial still enrolling)
'metabolic health' / longevity regimens in concierge practices
pediatric under-12 use under specialist care
drugs.pipeline_note: FICTIONAL. next_gen_launch (monthly_or_implant) is met by MariTide, which was under review at the start. FDA approved it in Feb 2033 after 72-week DEXA data: ≈20% mean loss, a body-composition monitoring requirement, and a label note that the antibody's long half-life means effects persist ~2 months after the last dose. It is given in clinic or pharmacy, and adherence is recorded at administration. No implant is on the US market. Survodutide (PDUFA early 2033) was approved Mar 2033 for weight and MASH. new_indications (compulsive_behaviour) cannot be an approval in this window because no trial was registered at the start. It is realised as a filing: in Mar 2034 Novo filed an sNDA for oral semaglutide in gambling disorder, based on two academic RCTs (Copenhagen, Toronto; 2031–33) plus a 26-week sponsor study. FDA granted priority review, and the PDUFA date is Feb 2035. Bimagrumab + semaglutide was filed Jun 2034, so approval is no earlier than mid-2035; it is the most watched file because it spares lean mass. The smoking-cessation SHAPS trial is still enrolling. Lilly's monthly and implant programmes are in phase 2 and not on the market.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Still the most common effect and the leading cause of voluntary stops. MariTide's first doses carry high vomiting rates, which slow-titration protocols reduce.
Rising in absolute numbers with a larger and older user base.
No causal confirmation; absolute risk low. Counterfeit product still confounds reporting.

A recognised population problem. A 2034 Medicare claims update estimates ≈2.0M long-term users aged 65+ meet sarcopenia criteria, up from ≈1.3M. In untrained users over 50, lean mass is ~30–40% of weight lost.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Class-wide Warnings and Precautions added Nov 2033. Baseline body-composition assessment is recommended for users 50+. MA strength benefits are near-universal. Lean-mass-sparing combinations are under review.

safety_ledger.effect: Bone mineral density loss and fragility fracture
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Third year of the wave. ≈8.5M users aged 65+ have more than 2 years' use. At ~0.6%/yr baseline hip-fracture rate × 0.35 excess, that is ≈17,900 excess hip fractures a year against ~305,000 US total, plus a rising vertebral tail in cycling women 50–64. DEXA waits are 10–16 weeks after capacity additions.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Class-wide bone Warnings and Precautions (Nov 2033). CMS extended the bone pause to 180 days and accepted REMS ultrasound as an interim substitute where DEXA wait exceeds 12 weeks. Private gated plans are still not bound. The DOJ civil case against Novo is unresolved.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Cohorts still conflict; absolute risk very low.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: EMA 'very rare' label; FDA warnings mention; no class determination.

safety_ledger.effect: Reward blunting / emotional flattening ('Ozempic personality', anhedonia, 'the grey')
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: ~12% of 12 mg retatrutide users cross a SHAPS threshold versus ~5% of comparators. An NIH-funded cohort (2034) gives the first independent low-dose read: a small mean SHAPS shift in 'calm' subscribers, no threshold excess, and a short follow-up. The effect is the mechanism behind the gambling sNDA, which makes regulators treat it as a feature and a harm at once.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: FTC consent orders stand. FDA asked for SHAPS data in the gambling sNDA review. No label change.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Millions of regain episodes a year from gating, verification misses and bone pauses. Regain is slower after MariTide because of the long tail.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: The 180-day bone pause softens it for Medicare. The Seventh Circuit upheld the Indiana waiver in 2033, and cert is pending.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Iron, B12, vitamin D, calcium and protein insufficiency are common in high-loss older users.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Professional guidance; Part D counselling template screen. No FDA action.

safety_ledger.effect: Long-horizon effects beyond ~10 years; adolescent exposure; repeated on/off cycling
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: About twelve years of follow-up. Full adolescent bone data were submitted in 2034 and are under review. Cycling still looks worse for bone than continuous use.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Postmarketing requirements continue; FDA advisory committee on adolescent bone scheduled for 2035.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Poison-centre calls are up ~10% since 2032 as imports rose to ≈4.7M users after the generic failure. Steady dosing-error and infection cases continue.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Import alerts and seizures continue. The 'Safe Pens' bill was reintroduced and stalled again. Individuals are still not prosecuted.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: A few percent, higher at 12 mg; usually transient.

safety_ledger.effect: Falls and frailty-related injury in older users
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Fall-related ED visits remain elevated in 65+ users with more than 2 years' use. Absolute numbers are rising with the 65+ user base.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Fall-risk screening is mandatory in the Part D counselling visit.

safety_ledger.effect: Adverse body-composition cycling (fat-dominant regain after lean-dominant loss)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Upgraded from emerging. Multiple DEXA cohorts confirm that repeated cycles leave users at the same weight with less lean mass and more visceral fat, worst in people over 50.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Cited in the Nov 2033 class labelling as the rationale for continuity. Advocates point out that gating causes it.

safety_ledger.effect: Heart-rate elevation at high triple-agonist doses
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: A mean resting heart-rate rise of several bpm at 12 mg retatrutide; arrhythmia significance unclear.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Labelled as a precaution; CVOT ongoing.

safety_ledger.effect: Prolonged drug effect after stopping monthly antibody (MariTide)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: New entry. Effects persist ~6–10 weeks after the last dose, so users cannot quickly stop for surgery, a severe GI episode or a 'grey' complaint. Anaesthesia societies report aspiration-precaution confusion.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Labelled. ASA guidance treats any MariTide dose in the prior 8 weeks as a full-stomach risk.

safety_ledger.effect: Bone density loss in premenopausal long-term users
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: New entry. Early cohorts of women 30–49 with more than 4 years' use show modest BMD deficits at hip and spine. Fracture significance is unknown.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Bone endpoints in women under 50 requested in postmarketing studies; no label change.

food_and_beverage.state: With a third of adults on the drug, salty-snack volume falls ~4%/yr and confectionery ~5%. Sugary drinks keep sliding. Growth is in protein, fortified dairy and 'bone-forward' lines, and also in a premium 'appetite' segment of butter, full-fat cheese, heritage pastry and steak aimed at unmedicated under-35s and holiday weekends. A third large group spun off its snack portfolio in 2033.

alcohol.state: Sixth straight year of US spirits volume decline, and beer is down. 'Holiday weekend' drinking creates spiky Friday–Sunday sales that distributors now plan around. Non-alcoholic formats are stable. Tobacco and vape keep falling faster than pre-2028 trend.

restaurants.state: Spend per cover is down ~10–12% from 2028 in high-uptake suburbs, and gram-priced bowls are standard. Two-tier dining has formed: weekday half portions, and weekend 'full table' or 'appetite room' nights in Brooklyn, Austin and Atlanta that sell out to unmedicated diners and users on a holiday. Value buffets keep closing.

apparel.state: Size churn continues, but monthly dosing slows it for some users. Fashion buyers now chase the trained shoulder: 'built' fits, structured upper-body tailoring and athletic cuts are growing, while slim-only mid-market lines are discounted. Rental and resale for cyclers persist.

fitness.state: Growing. Prescribed lifting is in nearly every MA plan, DEXA-plus-coaching chains are in strip malls, and young-adult 'fed lifting' gyms market eating as training. Staff qualified to train older lifters are still the binding constraint.

insurance.state: Employer coverage is 68%, and ~78% of it is gated, with stricter PDC than CMS. Pharmacy trend is ~+6% on volume at flat price. Fracture, fall and sarcopenia rehab costs are rising in Part A and MA. Some employers steer workers to MariTide because administered dosing satisfies their gating automatically. Wellness surcharges of up to 30% continue.

pharma.state: Volume up ~37% at flat prices. Lilly leads the weekly market, Amgen took ≈13M users with MariTide in under two years, Novo keeps Medicare semaglutide share, and Boehringer launched survodutide. Indian generic makers remain locked out of the US after the CRLs and are lobbying through the trade framework. Bone agents, DEXA and ultrasound makers keep winning.

body_and_culture.what_the_body_signals: Thinness has stopped signalling anything except coverage. With a third of adults on the drug and Medicaid paying for the bottom third, a lean body reads as 'enrolled'. The thin-armed forward stoop reads as an under-managed regimen and, increasingly, as low status. What is scarce now is muscle mass, visible appetite and the look of 'unmedicated vitality': thick shoulders, a full plate, an un-drugged laugh.
body_and_culture.thinness_and_class: Use levels have narrowed (bottom 31%, top 36%), and the class gap has moved to what a body shows. Top-third users display trained mass, DEXA on schedule and a public relish for food on holiday weekends. Bottom-third users are thin through Medicaid continuation standards, kiosk weigh-ins and long scan waits. Among under-30s in Austin, Brooklyn and Atlanta, 'never been on it' is a boast, and 'fed' is a compliment.
body_and_culture.eating_as_ritual: Protein-first weekday meals are the norm. Weekends have split: holiday-weekend 'full tables' are now a family institution, timed around oral doses, while monthly MariTide users sit them out or eat little. Church potlucks and no-gram rooms are fashionable again among young people who never ate in them.
body_and_culture.dating_and_intimacy: The on/off/pausing field on dating apps is standard, and 'unmedicated' has moved from niche filter to premium signal among under-30s. Couples argue about the holiday calendar: whether to take the weekend off together, and what happens when one partner is on a monthly shot and cannot.
body_and_culture.meaning_of_appetite: Appetite has been revalued. It is still treated medically, but it is also aestheticised as vitality, the thing cheap thinness took away. The backlash coalition (Atlanta body-sovereignty collectives, Tulsa–Dallas 'appetite is a gift' congregations, supplement influencers, disability advocates) has gained young members because its old message is now fashionable. Its political energy is still aimed at weigh-in welfare.

interior_life.reward_blunting_prevalence_note: FICTIONAL. 'The grey' is now a mainstream complaint rather than a shrug. A Sep 2034 national survey finds 41% of current oral and weekly users took at least one deliberate drug holiday in the past year, and 58% of them cite flatness rather than GI effects. Roughly 10M Americans are on top-dose triple, dual or 30%-class regimens, so the 12-vs-5% SHAPS gap implies ~700k excess cases of clinically meaningful anhedonia if causal. 'Calm' and 'focus' subscriptions plateaued at ≈4.0M as the complaint spread. The NIH cohort finds only a small mean shift at low dose. Monthly MariTide users cannot take holidays, and that is now its most common complaint.
interior_life.framing: Side effect in common speech, mechanism in the clinic, treatment in the gambling sNDA. People say 'I'm grey this month' the way they once said 'I'm burnt out'. Prescribers adjust doses for it routinely. Vendors have retreated from 'calm' toward 'steady'.
interior_life.effect_on_work: The holiday is part of office life: sales teams, chefs, performers and trial lawyers dose down before peaks, and HR calendars informally mark 'off weekends'. Gated employer plans requiring ≥90% PDC count a two-week holiday as non-adherence, so unions in hospitality and entertainment are bargaining for 'holiday allowances' modelled on the CMS 80% threshold. Some HR platforms have moved 'focus' subscriptions out of default catalogues. Warehouses and fleets prefer monthly administered dosing because it is verifiable.
interior_life.effect_on_art_and_play: Critics now talk about 'grey era' pop the way they once talked about loudness wars. 'Written on holiday' and 'unmedicated' are selling points in Nashville and on comedy tours, and no longer niche. Sports-betting handles in states paying for off-label gambling treatment flattened in 2034, and the leagues noticed. Extreme sports, spicy food and loud venues keep growing.
interior_life.effect_on_intimacy: Sex therapists build treatment around holiday calendars. Pharmacies stock 'restart' anti-nausea packs. Couples where one partner is on monthly MariTide describe being out of sync, unable to take the weekend off together, and clinicians now raise this when choosing a route.
interior_life.effect_on_politics: The 2034 midterms featured weigh-in welfare, DEXA waits and the failed generic. Populists of both parties attacked FDA's CRLs as protecting incumbents. Disability groups attacked administered-dose verification as surveillance. Senior groups won the 180-day bone pause. 'Calm voter' effects remain speculation, and the 'grey' complaint gave candidates a vocabulary for discontent they could not otherwise measure.

state.regulatory_posture: FDA is data-demanding and cautious: it requires DEXA in all filings, added class-wide bone and lean-mass warnings, sent CRLs to synthetic semaglutide ANDAs over immunogenicity, and gave the gambling sNDA priority review while asking for SHAPS data. Import enforcement is selective with no individual prosecutions. FTC acts on claims through consent orders.
state.subsidy_or_mandate: Public expansion continues. Permanent Part D obesity benefit at $199 with a $50 copay; 90% federal Medicaid match in 40 states plus DC; anti-obesity medication in 12 states' marketplace EHB benchmarks; problem-gambling funds in four states pay for off-label use. No individual mandate.
state.conditioning_or_surveillance: CMS 2034 continuation-standard update: a pharmacy-administered monthly dose counts as adherence and, when paired with the kiosk weight taken at administration, as the six-monthly verification. So MariTide users are verified twelve times a year by default. ≥80% PDC, ≥5% at 6 months or clinician override, annual DEXA or REMS ultrasound for long-term 65+ users, and a 180-day bone pause. Two missed verifications suspend coverage for 6 months. Indiana and Arkansas keep 12-month rules after the Seventh Circuit upheld them. Private gating covers ~78% of employer plans, often at 90% PDC and with no pause code. BMI-linked wellness surcharges of up to 30% continue.
state.workforce_or_military: DOT sleep-apnea screening still pushes drivers toward tirzepatide, and large fleets now prefer monthly MariTide with depot-administered doses. The Army adopted a 12-month-stability waiver like the Air Force's in 2033. Military recruiters report that 'fed' lifting culture among under-25s has modestly improved fitness pass rates.
state.geopolitics_of_supply: Chinese API and Indian finished product supply the world. After the CRLs India raised generic access under the 2032 trade framework, and FDA scheduled additional Hyderabad inspections. Section 232 tariffs remain. MariTide antibody manufacture in Ohio and Puerto Rico is the new capacity story, and Lilly's 12 mg allocation ended in mid-2033.

events.event: FDA approves Amgen's MariTide as a monthly weight-loss injection given at the pharmacy counter, with DEXA monitoring in the label; Medicare and Medicaid add it at the $199 rate after Amgen accepts the price in exchange for preferred placement

FDA sends complete-response letters to the leading generic semaglutide applications over peptide-impurity immunogenicity, and the 2033 settlement entry date passes with no generic on US shelves; portal prices stay at $199–279

CMS's 2034 rule counts a pharmacy-administered monthly dose and kiosk weight as verified adherence and extends the bone pause to 180 days; Pennsylvania, Michigan, Virginia, North Carolina and Arizona are among nine states taking the 90% Medicaid match by early 2034

FDA adds class-wide bone and muscle-loss warnings to all incretin weight drugs as a Medicare analysis puts excess hip fractures near 18,000 a year; CMS accepts ultrasound screening where DEXA waits exceed 12 weeks

Novo files to add gambling disorder to oral semaglutide's label and wins priority review, with a decision due February 2035; Ohio, New Jersey, Massachusetts and Illinois problem-gambling funds already pay for off-label prescriptions

A national survey finds 41% of users took a deliberate 'drug holiday' last year, most citing emotional flatness; the same month a sportswear giant's 'Eat Like You Mean It' line, modelled by unmedicated lifters, becomes its fastest seller

open_tensions: The generic cliff did not happen. FDA's immunogenicity CRLs kept US semaglutide branded and $199 through 2034, while ≈4.7M Americans inject Indian or Chinese pens at $5–30. Resubmissions, Indian trade pressure and a populist Congress converge on 2035, and the whole public bill (≈$84B gross across Medicare and Medicaid) is priced on an assumption that has already slipped once.

Monthly administered dosing turned adherence into an event the state records twelve times a year. MariTide users cannot take the holidays that 41% of other users rely on to escape 'the grey', and private plans at 90% PDC penalise oral users who do take them. Disability advocates call this surveillance, and employers call it efficiency.

Excess hip fractures are near 18,000 a year, ≈2.0M older users are sarcopenic, and a premenopausal bone signal is emerging. The drug is billed to Part D at $199, and the fractures and rehab go to Part A and MA. The 180-day bone pause protects Medicare users, while employer plans still cut off the same people for the same pause.

FDA must decide by Feb 2035 whether reward blunting is a treatment for gambling disorder at the same moment that the public names it as the drug's main psychological harm. Four states already pay for it with sports-betting revenue, and the industry they tax is watching.
still_true: No FDA-approved generic semaglutide or tirzepatide is on the US market; generic_us remains false.
Wegovy's list price remains $1,349 a month, and almost nobody pays it.
The permanent Part D obesity benefit still pays the $199/month negotiated rate with a $50 beneficiary copay and the counselling visit.
Oral starting doses (Wegovy pill, Foundayo) are still $149–150 a month cash through the federal direct-pricing portal (launched as TrumpRx) and manufacturer direct channels.
The suicidal-ideation warning removed from Wegovy, Zepbound and Saxenda labels in January 2026 has not returned.

prose.headline: Everyone's Thin Now. So Why Is Everyone Lifting, Eating, and Taking Weekends Off the Drug?
prose.world_in_600_words:
At the end of 2034 one American adult in three is on an incretin drug, and the body it produces no longer means much. For a decade thinness signalled money, discipline or luck. Now it mostly signals a Medicaid card or a gated plan. In 2034 the bottom income third is on the drug at nearly the rate of the top. What is scarce, and therefore desirable, is the body the drug does not make: heavy shoulders, a full plate, a person who has never been on it. Sportswear brands sell appetite. Under-thirties in Austin and Brooklyn treat 'unmedicated' as a boast. Restaurants in Atlanta sell out weekend 'appetite rooms' to people who are either off the drug or on holiday from it.

The holiday is the habit of the decade. Four in ten users of the weekly and oral drugs stopped on purpose at least once last year. Most did not say nausea. They said the grey, a flatness that is no longer embarrassing because everyone has felt it or lives with someone who has. Sales teams dose down before quarter's end. Couples plan weekends off together. Pop critics complain about a grey era of mid-tempo records.

The holiday is getting harder to take. Amgen's monthly shot, approved in February 2033, is given at the pharmacy counter, and its effect lingers for two months. Medicare and Medicaid took it at the same $199 rate as everything else, and CMS made each administered dose count as verified adherence, with the kiosk weight taken in the same visit. Thirteen million people now get their drug this way. Employers and fleets like it. Disability advocates call it weigh-in welfare made monthly. Users like the convenience and dislike that they cannot step off for a weekend.

Prices did not move. The generic semaglutide promised for 2033 never reached shelves after the FDA rejected the leading applications over peptide impurities. The portal still charges $199 to $279 for an injectable pen and $149 for a starter pill, and Wegovy's list price of $1,349 is still a number nobody pays. Nearly five million Americans inject pens mailed from Hyderabad and Shenzhen instead. Coverage grew anyway, through the public programmes: nine more states took the ninety-percent Medicaid match, a dozen marketplaces added the drugs, and Medicare's obesity benefit now serves eleven million people. Public programmes are now the default payer for the old and the poor.

The old are where the bill comes due. Medicare's own analysis puts the excess at roughly eighteen thousand hip fractures a year, and two million long-term older users meet criteria for sarcopenia. In November 2033 the FDA put bone and muscle warnings on every drug in the class. CMS doubled the bone pause to 180 days and, where scanners are booked past twelve weeks, accepts an ultrasound in place of a DEXA scan. Employer plans mostly did neither. A fifty-eight-year-old in Phoenix still loses coverage for following the advice her mother's Medicare plan pays for. The drug is billed to Part D at $199 a month. The broken hips are billed to Part A.

The flatness is also becoming a treatment. Four states spend sports-betting revenue on off-label semaglutide for problem gamblers, and Novo has filed to add gambling disorder to the label, with a decision due in February. Regulators will be asked to approve, for one population, the effect that users elsewhere take holidays to escape.

Nothing looks broken. The gyms are full and the grocery aisles are full of protein, and weekend dinners are crowded again. The new scarcity is a body the drug did not shape and a weekend it does not dull.
prose.a_day_in_the_life:
Tammy Kessler gets to the Kroger pharmacy on Brown Street in Dayton at 7:40, before her first client. It is the fourteenth of the month, which means the shot. She steps on the kiosk scale, puts her Medicaid card under the reader and watches 171.4 appear beside her photo. The pharmacist, a boy who calls her Miss Tammy, swabs her arm. Copay four dollars. The screen says VERIFIED and shows a green check.

She drives to Mrs. Albers in Kettering, who is eighty-three, on the weekly pen, and on her second bone pause. Mrs. Albers wants to know if the ultrasound counts now. Tammy says it does. She helps her into the shower chair and notices, as she does every week, how little of her arm there is.

At lunch she eats half a turkey wrap in the car and leaves the rest on the dash.

Cody comes for dinner Thursdays. He is twenty-seven, works nights at the Amazon building in Union, and has never been on anything. He brings a pound of ground chuck and a bag of rolls and cooks it himself, because she no longer cooks properly. He eats four sliders. His shoulders fill the kitchen doorway. His girlfriend posts him on Saturdays with the word fed.

He asks if she's coming to his cousin's on Sunday, the full table.

She says she just had her shot.

He says, so take next month off.

She says you can't, with this one, it stays in you.

He nods and wipes the grease off his plate with a roll. She watches him chew. She can't remember the last time she felt like that about food.
